title: Hugues Panassie's 1938 visit and his heroes
summary: Russell recalls Panassie's trip to New York, his refusal to go to Chicago, his admiration for Mezzrow and Fats Waller, and his money.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: no he didn't come down here no and he didn't even go to Chicago I was sort of disgusted myself he'd had me to talk to Carl Cons who was editor of Downbeat then tried to get him a few lectures or something so he could get enough money to go to Chicago and he wanted to see Jimmy Noon by that time was his big hero in his first book he'd talk more about the so called Chicago style Teichmacher and others
did he call it that or did he call it

Chicago style yeah I would say he's responsible for that term more than anybody I think one chapter of his maybe was called Chicago style if I remember I haven't looked at the book for many years but anyway you'd think that he would have wanted to go to Chicago and meet Jimmy Noon and the Dodds brothers no there were dozens of good musicians there then at least a dozen safe in New Orleans people like Natty Dominic and others but it was either he was too tight or didn't want to make the trip of course he was somewhat crippled and didn't get around quite as easily as some people
and we found out later when he was ready to go back that he had quite a bit of money in the bank and he could easily have made the trip himself
but I don't know who did he see in New York

do you remember oh everybody from Fats Waller of course was one of his big favorites too there's several pictures taken of him listening to Fats Waller I know and there's a picture I just got the other day I got Eddie Condon's scrapbook there's a picture of him sitting there with somebody was it like Duke Ellington or somebody I believe at some club listening to Mez and other people I don't know how they all got together that way but anyway Mez Mesro was one of his favorites he lived up in Harlem with Mez Mez was married to a black girl and had a son see Mez was always sorry he wasn't black I guess I noticed Eddie Condon again reading this book for the first time always talking about Mez and his phony southern accent I never
